ambiguous.why: Classic crypto-ransomware denies access, so Availability is the primary loss. But modern ransomware is double-extortion (exfiltrate, then encrypt), and a practitioner could defensibly say the primary attack is on Confidentiality; a third reading calls encryption of data-in-place an unauthorised modification, i.e. Integrity.

misleading_hints.hint: If two legs seem to fit, ask which loss the victim notices first, and which one they could still be suffering without knowing.
misleading_hints.why: The hint sets up a two-way test (noticed-immediately = Availability, suffered-silently = Confidentiality) that has no slot for silent Integrity loss. Applied literally to 'Payroll figures silently altered in the database' — the textbook Integrity item — the 'suffering without knowing' clause steers the learner to Confidentiality.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties is a managerial/administrative principle, which is why I marked it IN. A practitioner who reads the item as the enforcement mechanism in the payments application (dual-approval workflow configured in software) would call it technical and mark it OUT.

ambiguous.item: You refuse to scan a network you have no written authorisation to test
ambiguous.alternative: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
ambiguous.why: I read the situation as being about the practitioner's own legality (unauthorised scanning is unlawful), which is Canon II. A practitioner could equally argue it is fundamentally about not endangering someone else's infrastructure, which is Canon I.

ambiguous.item: You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Conflict-of-interest avoidance is stated under the duty owed to principals (Canon III), which is why I placed it there. But 'avoid apparent or actual conflicts of interest' is also read as a matter of personal honour and justice, giving a defensible Canon II answer.

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: The act is personal honesty (Canon II), but FUD-selling is also the classic example of conduct that damages the standing and reputation of the security profession, so Canon IV is defensible.

ambiguous.item: Every system must have a named owner who is accountable for its security
ambiguous.why: It is mandatory and organisation-wide but assigns accountability rather than specifying a technology, which reads as Policy. A practitioner who applies the 'mandatory + specific requirement = Standard' test literally would call it a Standard, since it states a concrete, testable requirement rather than an intention.
